newsitem.title: UK: UK gilt repo ready for central monetary role.
newsitem.headline: UK gilt repo ready for central monetary role.

text.p: The UK gilt repo market, set up at the start of 1996, has blossomed over the course of the year and is now well-rooted enough to allow the Bank of England to use it as the centrepiece of its monetary operations.
European central banks, particularly the Bundesbank, have long used repos to intervene in the money markets and signal interest rate changes. Britain could soon follow suit.
The Bank of England released a paper earlier this month showing its readiness to include gilt repos in its daily money market operations from early next year.
Bank of England executive director Ian Plenderleith said the Bank's proposals took account of the successful development of the repo market.

A by-product is that the use of gilt repos in daily operations is consistent with proposals under discussion at the European Monetary Institute, the forerunner of the proposed European central bank, Plenderleith said.
"This is the big issue for the repo market -- when will the Bank start to use the repo rate as the central one for its operations," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International.
"The market has become active enough to become the lynchpin of the monetary system. It certainly has sufficient liquidity and depth," he added.
OFFICIAL FIGURES SHOW RAPIDLY EXPANDING MARKET

Latest figures from the Bank all show an expanding market. For the three months to the end of August outstanding repo and stock lending leapt to 80 billion pounds, from around 50 billion over the three months to end-May.
Daily turnover in gilt repos has reached at least 15 billion pounds a day. In the previous quarter, turnover was below seven billion.
"The gilt repo market has moved on from its phase of consolidation in the spring, helping to attract new participants into the market," the Bank said.
A repo is an agreement to sell a bond at a given interest rate for a specified period, with the agreement that the original holder buys it back at the end of that time.
REPOS ALLOW ALL INVESTORS TO SHORT GILTS
Until this year, Britain was one of the few major financial centres without a repo market. The authorities launched one, partly to lure more investors, particularly from overseas.
As a result, gilt investors can now take short gilt positions. Previously, only gilt-edged market-makers (GEMMS) and discount houses were allowed to do so.

The rise in repo business suggests at least some investors have taken advantage of their new ability to short gilts -- a good bet, given the uncertainty created by looming elections, Britain's aloofness from a single European currency and the prospect of higher interest rates.
BUT BENEFITS TO GILT YIELDS NEGLIGIBLE SO FAR
But although the repo market has made gilts more attractive, the benefits in yield terms have probably been small.
"One suspects that the current gilt/Bund spread probably wouldn't be very different from now without the repo market," said Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc.

The marginal gains to the overall gilt market of the introduction of repo facilities have been greatly outweighed by the gnawing political uncertainty surrounding a government now robbed of its parliamentary majority, not to mention the right to opt out of a European single currency.
INSTITUTIONAL INVESTORS YET TO TAKE REPO BAIT
And from a trading perspective, experts said the repo market still has a long way to go.
"The market has matched expectations to an extent but the lack of institutional investors in the market has been disappointing," said Valerie Keats, gilt repo specialist at Societe Generale.
"The market is dominated by too few players at the moment."
She said the increasing number of bonds trading "on special" in the repo market may generate more interest.

If a gilt stock is in short supply it can be repoed out far more expensively than prevailing repo market rates. On occasions this year, certain stocks have traded several hundred basis points through the market's general collateral rates. But these instances need to become more frequent.
"Specials are good news for the market but the big squeezes that have gone on so far have been dominated by one or two large players doing it for the hell of it," one repo trader said.
